name: Great saphenous vein
func: The longest vein in the body. It runs just under the skin from the inner side of the foot up the inner leg and thigh, draining the skin and fat of the leg into the deep femoral vein near the groin.

levels.kid:
The **great saphenous vein** is the longest vein in your whole body! It starts on the inside of your foot, near your ankle bone, and climbs all the way up the inside of your leg to the top of your thigh.

It lives just under your skin. Sometimes you can even see it as a faint bluish line on the inside of your ankle.

Its job is to carry used blood from your skin and the soft layer under it back up toward your heart. Going uphill is hard, so it has tiny one-way doors inside, called valves, that stop the blood from sliding back down.
levels.hs:
The **great saphenous vein (GSV)** is a **superficial vein**: it runs in the fatty layer just under the skin, outside the deep muscle compartments. It begins from the **medial end of the dorsal venous arch** of the foot and passes **in front of the medial malleolus** (the bony bump on the inside of the ankle), a very reliable landmark.

It then climbs the **medial side of the leg**, accompanied by the **saphenous nerve** (which carries feeling from the inner leg). It passes about a hand's breadth behind the inner edge of the kneecap, behind the medial side of the knee, then runs up the inner and front side of the thigh.

About 3–4 cm below and lateral to the pubic tubercle, it dives through an opening in the deep fascia called the **saphenous opening** to join the **femoral vein** at the **saphenofemoral junction**.

The GSV contains about 10–20 **valves** that keep blood flowing upward. **Perforating veins** connect it to the deep veins, and their valves normally let blood pass only from superficial to deep, where the squeezing of calf muscles pumps it back toward the heart.
levels.college:
Near the saphenofemoral junction, the GSV receives several tributaries: the **superficial epigastric**, **superficial circumflex iliac** veins, plus accessory saphenous veins from the thigh. The junction itself has a **terminal valve** and a **preterminal valve** a few centimetres below.

The **small saphenous vein** is its partner: it starts at the lateral end of the dorsal arch, passes **behind the lateral malleolus**, runs up the back of the calf with the **sural nerve**, and usually joins the **popliteal vein** behind the knee.

The **saphenous nerve** is closely applied to the GSV below the knee, so it can be injured during vein harvesting or stripping, causing numbness of the inner leg and foot.

The **muscle pump**: when the calf muscles contract inside their tight fascia, they compress deep veins and push blood upward; valves stop backflow. When they relax, pressure in the deep veins falls, and blood flows in from the superficial system through perforators. Walking drops pressure in ankle veins from about 90 mmHg (standing still, a column of blood) to around 20–30 mmHg.

On ultrasound, the GSV sits within its own fascial compartment, the **saphenous eye** (an "eye" shape formed by superficial and deep fascia), which helps distinguish it from tributaries.

Because of its length and accessibility, it's the most-used vein for **coronary bypass grafts** and for leg artery bypass.
levels.phd:
Venous valves are thin bicuspid folds of endothelium-covered connective tissue, but they're metabolically and mechanically special. The **valve sinus** (the pocket behind each cusp) has vortical, slow flow and relatively **low oxygen tension**, and valve endothelium expresses distinctive anticoagulant proteins (high **thrombomodulin** and **endothelial protein C receptor**, low von Willebrand factor). Valve formation depends on developmental genes such as **PROX1**, **FOXC2** and **GJC2**, shared with lymphatic valves; **FOXC2** mutations cause **lymphedema–distichiasis**, which also features venous valve failure.

In **chronic venous disease**, persistent **venous hypertension** alters shear stress: endothelial cells become activated, leukocytes adhere and migrate into the wall, and **MMPs** degrade the matrix. The wall becomes thickened in some areas and thinned in others, with disorganized smooth muscle and collagen, and valve cusps stretch, thin or tear, causing **reflux**. Whether wall weakness precedes valve failure or vice versa is still debated; both probably reinforce each other.

In the skin, high capillary pressure leaks fibrinogen and red cells; iron from broken-down hemoglobin (**hemosiderin**) stains the skin brown, and chronic inflammation causes **lipodermatosclerosis** (woody fibrosis) and eventually **venous ulcers**.

As a bypass graft, the GSV undergoes **arterialization**: it faces arterial pressure and shear for the first time, triggering **intimal hyperplasia** (smooth muscle proliferation and matrix deposition). This, plus later accelerated atherosclerosis, explains why vein grafts fail more often than internal thoracic artery grafts over 10 years.
levels.expert:
**Varicose veins** are dilated, twisting superficial veins, most commonly from **GSV reflux** at the saphenofemoral junction. Symptoms include aching, heaviness, itching and swelling worse at day's end. Examination: inspect standing; the old **Trendelenburg** and **tourniquet tests** localize incompetent valves, but **duplex ultrasound** (reflux longer than 0.5 seconds) has replaced them. Signs of advanced disease (CEAP classification) include ankle swelling, **brown skin staining**, eczema, lipodermatosclerosis and **venous ulcers** above the medial malleolus.

**Superficial thrombophlebitis** is a tender, red, cord-like vein. It's important because clot near the saphenofemoral junction can extend into the deep femoral vein, leading to **DVT** and **pulmonary embolism**.

The GSV in front of the medial malleolus is the classic site for an emergency **venous cutdown** when other IV access is impossible.

In **coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG)**, the GSV is harvested (open or endoscopically) as a conduit; leg wound problems and **saphenous nerve** numbness are known complications. Surgeons check the vein on ultrasound beforehand, since prior stripping or varicose disease makes it unusable.

Treatment in general terms: **compression stockings**, leg elevation and exercise; **endovenous thermal ablation** (laser or radiofrequency heat sealing the vein from inside), foam sclerotherapy or cyanoacrylate glue closure; and surgical ligation and stripping, now less common. Venous ulcers heal best with compression plus treating the underlying reflux.

keyPoints: Longest vein in the body; superficial, on the medial leg
Passes in front of the medial malleolus (reliable cutdown site)
Joins the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction in the groin
Valves + calf muscle pump keep blood moving upward
Reflux causes varicose veins; diagnosed by duplex ultrasound
Most-used conduit for coronary and leg bypass grafts

test.q: The great saphenous vein passes which landmark at the ankle?
choices: In front of the medial malleolus
test.explain: Anterior to the medial malleolus, a reliable spot for venous access; the small saphenous passes behind the lateral malleolus.

test.q: The great saphenous vein drains into which deep vein in the groin?
test.explain: At the saphenofemoral junction, through the saphenous opening.

test.q: Which nerve runs beside the GSV below the knee and can be injured when the vein is harvested?
test.explain: The saphenous nerve (branch of the femoral) supplies skin of the inner leg and foot.

test.q: Dilated, twisted superficial leg veins from valve failure are:
test.explain: Usually from reflux at the saphenofemoral junction.

test.q: The GSV is commonly harvested as a conduit for coronary artery ______ grafting.
test.explain: Its length and accessibility make it ideal, though arterial grafts last longer.

test.q: Calf muscle contraction moves blood upward mainly because of:
test.explain: Valves prevent backflow so squeezing can only push blood toward the heart.
